claim: Latrophilins were originally identified as responders to α-latrotoxin, a neurotoxin from black widow spider venom that causes the profound release of neurotransmitters from nerve terminals.
source: They belong to the family of adhesion G protein-coupled receptors (aGPCRs), capable of eliciting intracellular effects through coupling with heterotrimeric G proteins (Lelianova et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Davletov et al., 1996

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Boucard et al., 2012

claim: Latrophilins have been implicated in neuronal migration in the central nervous system.
source: In the central nervous system, latrophilins have been implicated in neuronal migration, circuit assembly, and synapse formation (Anderson et al., 2017; Del Toro et al., 2020; Donohue et al., 2021; Pederick et al., 2021; Sando et al., 2019; Sando and Südhof, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2017; Del Toro et al., 2020; Donohue et al., 2021; Pederick et al., 2021; Sando et al., 2019; Sando and Südhof, 2021

claim: Latrophilins have been implicated in circuit assembly in the central nervous system.
source: In the central nervous system, latrophilins have been implicated in neuronal migration, circuit assembly, and synapse formation (Anderson et al., 2017; Del Toro et al., 2020; Donohue et al., 2021; Pederick et al., 2021; Sando et al., 2019; Sando and Südhof, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2017; Del Toro et al., 2020; Donohue et al., 2021; Pederick et al., 2021; Sando et al., 2019; Sando and Südhof, 2021

claim: Latrophilins have been implicated in synapse formation in the central nervous system.
source: In the central nervous system, latrophilins have been implicated in neuronal migration, circuit assembly, and synapse formation (Anderson et al., 2017; Del Toro et al., 2020; Donohue et al., 2021; Pederick et al., 2021; Sando et al., 2019; Sando and Südhof, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2017; Del Toro et al., 2020; Donohue et al., 2021; Pederick et al., 2021; Sando et al., 2019; Sando and Südhof, 2021

claim: Polymorphisms in LPHN3 are associated with an increased risk of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in humans.
source: In humans, polymorphisms in LPHN3 are associated with an increased risk of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, and a missense variant in the LPHN2 gene is responsible for extreme microcephaly (Arcos-Burgos et al., 2010; Domené et al., 2011; Vezain et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Arcos-Burgos et al., 2010; Domené et al., 2011

claim: A missense variant in the LPHN2 gene is responsible for extreme microcephaly in humans.
source: In humans, polymorphisms in LPHN3 are associated with an increased risk of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, and a missense variant in the LPHN2 gene is responsible for extreme microcephaly (Arcos-Burgos et al., 2010; Domené et al., 2011; Vezain et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vezain et al., 2018

claim: Lphn2 displays expression patterns inverse to teneurin-3 (Ten3) in two parallel hippocampal networks in mice.
source: We recently showed in mice that one of the three latrophilins, Lphn2, displays expression patterns inverse to teneurin-3 (Ten3) in two parallel hippocampal networks (Pederick et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pederick et al., 2021

claim: Hippocampal Lphn2 is preferentially expressed in the distal CA1 and the proximal subiculum.
source: While hippocampal Lphn2 is preferentially expressed in the distal CA1 and the proximal subiculum, Ten3 is enriched in the proximal CA1 and the distal subiculum.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pederick et al., 2021 in the preceding sentence

claim: Ten3 is enriched in the proximal CA1 and the distal subiculum.
source: While hippocampal Lphn2 is preferentially expressed in the distal CA1 and the proximal subiculum, Ten3 is enriched in the proximal CA1 and the distal subiculum.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pederick et al., 2021 in the preceding sentence

claim: Expression patterns and reciprocal repulsions mediated by Ten3-Lphn2 interactions instruct proximal CA1 axons to target the distal subiculum.
source: These expression patterns and reciprocal repulsions mediated by Ten3-Lphn2 interactions instruct proximal CA1 axons to target the distal subiculum, and more distal CA1 axons to target more proximal subiculum (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pederick et al., 2021 in the preceding context

claim: Expression patterns and reciprocal repulsions mediated by Ten3-Lphn2 interactions instruct more distal CA1 axons to target more proximal subiculum.
source: These expression patterns and reciprocal repulsions mediated by Ten3-Lphn2 interactions instruct proximal CA1 axons to target the distal subiculum, and more distal CA1 axons to target more proximal subiculum (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pederick et al., 2021 in the preceding context

claim: Lphn2 acts as a 'receptor' in more distal CA1 axons that is repelled by Ten3 expressed from the distal subiculum.
source: Specifically, Lphn2 acts as a 'receptor' in more distal CA1 axons that is repelled by Ten3 expressed from the distal subiculum (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pederick et al., 2021 in the preceding context

claim: Lphn2 acts as a repulsive 'ligand' in the proximal subiculum to repel Ten3-expressing proximal CA1 axons.
source: At the same time, Lphn2 acts as a repulsive 'ligand' in the proximal subiculum to repel Ten3-expressing (Ten3+) proximal CA1 axons; this action requires Lphn2's teneurin-binding domain but not its FLRT-binding activity (Figure 1C; Pederick et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pederick et al., 2021

claim: Lphn2's action as a repulsive ligand in the proximal subiculum requires Lphn2's teneurin-binding domain but not its FLRT-binding activity.
source: At the same time, Lphn2 acts as a repulsive 'ligand' in the proximal subiculum to repel Ten3-expressing (Ten3+) proximal CA1 axons; this action requires Lphn2's teneurin-binding domain but not its FLRT-binding activity (Figure 1C; Pederick et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pederick et al., 2021

claim: Lphn2 is required cell autonomously as a receptor in more distal CA1 axons for their precise target selection.
source: Therefore, Lphn2 is required cell autonomously as a receptor in more distal CA1 axons for their precise target selection, and non-autonomously in target neurons as a ligand for precise target selection of proximal CA1 axons.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pederick et al., 2021 in the preceding context

claim: Lphn2 is required non-autonomously in target neurons as a ligand for precise target selection of proximal CA1 axons.
source: Therefore, Lphn2 is required cell autonomously as a receptor in more distal CA1 axons for their precise target selection, and non-autonomously in target neurons as a ligand for precise target selection of proximal CA1 axons.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pederick et al., 2021 in the preceding context

claim: Ten3 mediates homophilic attraction.
source: While Ten3 additionally mediates homophilic attraction (Berns et al., 2018; Pederick et al., 2021), Lphn2 does not mediate homophilic binding in trans (Boucard et al., 2014; Pederick et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Berns et al., 2018; Pederick et al., 2021

claim: Lphn2 does not mediate homophilic binding in trans.
source: While Ten3 additionally mediates homophilic attraction (Berns et al., 2018; Pederick et al., 2021), Lphn2 does not mediate homophilic binding in trans (Boucard et al., 2014; Pederick et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Boucard et al., 2014; Pederick et al., 2021

claim: The N-terminal extracellular domain of latrophilins comprises a rhamnose-binding lectin (RBL) domain.
source: Structurally, the N-terminal extracellular domain of latrophilins comprises a rhamnose-binding lectin (RBL) domain, an olfactomedin-like (OLF) ligand-binding domain, a serine/threonine-rich region and hormone receptor motif (HRM), and a conserved GPCR autoproteolysis-inducing (GAIN) domain that encompasses the GPCR proteolysis site (GPS) (Araç et al., 2012; Moreno-Salinas et al., 2019; Vizurraga et al., 2020; Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Araç et al., 2012; Moreno-Salinas et al., 2019; Vizurraga et al., 2020

claim: The N-terminal extracellular domain of latrophilins comprises an olfactomedin-like (OLF) ligand-binding domain.
source: Structurally, the N-terminal extracellular domain of latrophilins comprises a rhamnose-binding lectin (RBL) domain, an olfactomedin-like (OLF) ligand-binding domain, a serine/threonine-rich region and hormone receptor motif (HRM), and a conserved GPCR autoproteolysis-inducing (GAIN) domain that encompasses the GPCR proteolysis site (GPS) (Araç et al., 2012; Moreno-Salinas et al., 2019; Vizurraga et al., 2020; Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Araç et al., 2012; Moreno-Salinas et al., 2019; Vizurraga et al., 2020

claim: The N-terminal extracellular domain of latrophilins comprises a serine/threonine-rich region and hormone receptor motif (HRM).
source: Structurally, the N-terminal extracellular domain of latrophilins comprises a rhamnose-binding lectin (RBL) domain, an olfactomedin-like (OLF) ligand-binding domain, a serine/threonine-rich region and hormone receptor motif (HRM), and a conserved GPCR autoproteolysis-inducing (GAIN) domain that encompasses the GPCR proteolysis site (GPS) (Araç et al., 2012; Moreno-Salinas et al., 2019; Vizurraga et al., 2020; Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Araç et al., 2012; Moreno-Salinas et al., 2019; Vizurraga et al., 2020

claim: The N-terminal extracellular domain of latrophilins comprises a conserved GPCR autoproteolysis-inducing (GAIN) domain that encompasses the GPCR proteolysis site (GPS).
source: Structurally, the N-terminal extracellular domain of latrophilins comprises a rhamnose-binding lectin (RBL) domain, an olfactomedin-like (OLF) ligand-binding domain, a serine/threonine-rich region and hormone receptor motif (HRM), and a conserved GPCR autoproteolysis-inducing (GAIN) domain that encompasses the GPCR proteolysis site (GPS) (Araç et al., 2012; Moreno-Salinas et al., 2019; Vizurraga et al., 2020; Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Araç et al., 2012; Moreno-Salinas et al., 2019; Vizurraga et al., 2020

claim: aGPCRs undergo autoproteolytic cleavage at the HL/T consensus site within the GPS.
source: aGPCRs undergo autoproteolytic cleavage at the HL/T consensus site within the GPS.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Araç et al., 2012; Moreno-Salinas et al., 2019; Vizurraga et al., 2020 in the preceding sentence

claim: Self-cleavage of aGPCRs divides the receptor into an extracellular N-terminal fragment (NTF) and a membrane-bound C-terminal fragment (CTF) that remain noncovalently associated throughout biosynthesis and membrane trafficking.
source: This self-cleavage divides the receptor into an extracellular N-terminal fragment (NTF) and a membrane-bound C-terminal fragment (CTF) that remain noncovalently associated throughout biosynthesis and membrane trafficking (Vizurraga et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vizurraga et al., 2020

claim: The seven residues immediately C-terminal to the GPS constitute the tethered agonist peptide.
source: The seven residues immediately C-terminal to the GPS constitute the tethered agonist peptide (also known as the Stachel or stalk peptide), which upon exposure binds within the transmembrane domain to activate heterotrimeric G proteins (Liebscher and Schöneberg, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liebscher and Schöneberg, 2016

claim: The tethered agonist peptide upon exposure binds within the transmembrane domain to activate heterotrimeric G proteins.
source: The seven residues immediately C-terminal to the GPS constitute the tethered agonist peptide (also known as the Stachel or stalk peptide), which upon exposure binds within the transmembrane domain to activate heterotrimeric G proteins (Liebscher and Schöneberg, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liebscher and Schöneberg, 2016

claim: Lphn2 couples to Gα12/13 in heterologous cells.
source: Here, we show that Lphn2 couples to Gα12/13 in heterologous cells; this coupling is increased by constitutive exposure of the tethered agonist.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Lphn2 coupling to Gα12/13 is increased by constitutive exposure of the tethered agonist.
source: Here, we show that Lphn2 couples to Gα12/13 in heterologous cells; this coupling is increased by constitutive exposure of the tethered agonist.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and 2E

claim: Specific mutations of Lphn2's tethered agonist region disrupt its G protein coupling.
source: Specific mutations of Lphn2's tethered agonist region disrupt its G protein coupling and autoproteolytic cleavage, whereas mutating the autoproteolytic cleavage site alone prevents cleavage but preserves a functional tethered agonist.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4

claim: Specific mutations of Lphn2's tethered agonist region disrupt its autoproteolytic cleavage.
source: Specific mutations of Lphn2's tethered agonist region disrupt its G protein coupling and autoproteolytic cleavage, whereas mutating the autoproteolytic cleavage site alone prevents cleavage but preserves a functional tethered agonist.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Mutating the autoproteolytic cleavage site alone prevents cleavage but preserves a functional tethered agonist.
source: Specific mutations of Lphn2's tethered agonist region disrupt its G protein coupling and autoproteolytic cleavage, whereas mutating the autoproteolytic cleavage site alone prevents cleavage but preserves a functional tethered agonist.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: Wild-type Lphn2 misdirects proximal CA1 axons to the proximal subiculum when misexpressed in proximal CA1.
source: Using an in vivo misexpression assay, we demonstrate that wild-type Lphn2 misdirects proximal CA1 axons to the proximal subiculum and that Lphn2 tethered agonist activity is required for its role as a repulsive receptor in axons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1

claim: Lphn2 tethered agonist activity is required for its role as a repulsive receptor in axons.
source: Using an in vivo misexpression assay, we demonstrate that wild-type Lphn2 misdirects proximal CA1 axons to the proximal subiculum and that Lphn2 tethered agonist activity is required for its role as a repulsive receptor in axons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4

claim: Neither tethered agonist activity nor autoproteolysis were necessary for Lphn2's role as a repulsive ligand in the subiculum target neurons.
source: By contrast, neither tethered agonist activity nor autoproteolysis were necessary for Lphn2's role as a repulsive ligand in the subiculum target neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5

claim: Tethered agonist activity is required for Lphn2-mediated neural circuit assembly in a context-dependent manner.
source: Thus, tethered agonist activity is required for Lphn2-mediated neural circuit assembly in a context-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3, 4, and 5

claim: Lphn2-CTF significantly enhanced signaling over wild-type Lphn2 for SRE gene expression at varying levels of cDNA transfection.
source: We found that Lphn2-CTF significantly enhanced signaling over wild-type Lphn2 for SRE gene expression at varying levels of cDNA transfection (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Lphn2 signals through Gα12/13 rather than Gαq.
source: Since the SRE assay reports on signaling by Gα12/13 as well as Gαq we tested whether Gα12/13 or Gαq was the primary contributor to this response using a selective Gαq inhibitor, YM-254890 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). We did not observe a significant effect upon the addition of the inhibitor, suggesting that Lphn2 signals through Gα12/13.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: When Gα12 or Gα13 was re-introduced to cells expressing the Lphn2 construct there was a significant increase in the BRET signal upon treatment with enterokinase.
source: As expected, in the absence of Gα subunits no BRET signal was observed; however, when Gα12 or Gα13 was re-introduced to cells expressing the Lphn2 construct there was a significant increase in the BRET signal upon treatment with enterokinase (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: No increase in BRET signal was observed upon co-expression of the Lphn2 receptor with Gαs, Gαi1, or Gαq.
source: This increase was not observed upon co-expression of the receptor with Gαs, Gαi1, or Gαq (Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Lphn2 signals through the G proteins Gα12 and Gα13 in heterologous cells.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that Lphn2 signals through the G proteins Gα12 and Gα13 in heterologous cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2

claim: Mutating phenylalanine (F831) and methionine (M835) to alanine (F831A/M835A) would impair G protein signaling mediated by the tethered agonist.
source: We hypothesized that mutating these residues in Lphn2, phenylalanine (F831), and methionine (M835), to alanine (F831A/M835A) would impair G protein signaling mediated by the tethered agonist (Figure 3A).
evidence: The hypothesis is based on previous studies suggesting that the third and seventh residues of aGPCRs are required for tethered agonist-mediated G protein activation (Stoveken et al., 2015)

claim: Lphn2_F831A/M835A is largely uncleaved.
source: Immunoblotting against the C-terminal FLAG-tag confirmed expression in HEK293T cells but showed that Lphn2_F831A/M835A is largely uncleaved (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Mutating the third phenylalanine to an alanine disrupts autoproteolytic cleavage in Lphn1.
source: This is consistent with previous work with Lphn1 showing that mutating the third phenylalanine to an alanine disrupts autoproteolytic cleavage (Araç et al., 2012) and shows that the double mutation (F831A/M835A) in Lphn2 also inhibits cleavage.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Araç et al., 2012

claim: The double mutation (F831A/M835A) in Lphn2 inhibits cleavage.
source: This is consistent with previous work with Lphn1 showing that mutating the third phenylalanine to an alanine disrupts autoproteolytic cleavage (Araç et al., 2012) and shows that the double mutation (F831A/M835A) in Lphn2 also inhibits cleavage.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Lphn2_F831A/M835A is expressed on the cell surface at a comparable level as Lphn2 wild-type.
source: We also validated that Lphn2_F831A/M835A is expressed on the cell surface at a comparable level as Lphn2 wild-type (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Both the full-length Lphn2_F831A/M835A and the Lphn2-CTF_F831A/M835A have dramatically impaired responses to SRE across varying levels of cDNA transfection.
source: As hypothesized, both the full-length and truncated Lphn2 had dramatically impaired responses to SRE across varying levels of cDNA transfection.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Lphn2-CTF_F831A/M835A did not yield a BRET signal after the re-introduction of any of the G proteins in question (Gαs, Gαi1, Gαq, Gα12, or Gα13).
source: Unlike the wild-type receptor, Lphn2-CTF_F831A/M835A did not yield a BRET signal after the re-introduction of any of the G proteins in question (Gαs, Gαi1, Gαq, Gα12, or Gα13) (Figure 3C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: The F831A/M835A mutations in Lphn2 impair tethered agonist-mediated G protein coupling.
source: Taken together, our findings demonstrate that the F831A/M835A mutations in Lphn2 impair tethered agonist-mediated G protein coupling.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: The majority of Lphn2_F831A/M835A-expressing proximal CA1 axons targeted the most distal third of the subiculum, like negative control Cre animals.
source: The majority of Lphn2_F831A/M835A-expressing proximal CA1 axons targeted the most distal third of the subiculum, like negative control Cre animals (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: The fraction of axon intensity in Cre-Lphn2_F831A/M835A animals was significantly lower in the proximal subiculum and significantly higher in the distal subiculum when compared to Cre-P2A-Lphn2 animals.
source: The fraction of axon intensity in Cre-Lphn2_F831A/M835A animals was significantly lower in the proximal subiculum and significantly higher in the distal subiculum when compared to Cre-P2A-Lphn2 animals (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E

claim: Tethered agonist activity or autoproteolysis is required for Lphn2-mediated miswiring of proximal CA1 axons.
source: Collectively, these findings suggest that tethered agonist activity or autoproteolysis is required for Lphn2-mediated miswiring of proximal CA1 axons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: Replacing threonine-838 in the tethered agonist of Lphn1 to glycine inhibited autoproteolysis while maintaining proper folding of the receptor.
source: Previous studies showed that replacing threonine-838 in the tethered agonist of Lphn1 or threonine-923 in the tethered agonist of Lphn3 to glycine inhibited autoproteolysis while maintaining proper folding of the receptor (Araç et al., 2012; Kordon et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Araç et al., 2012; Kordon et al., 2023

claim: Replacing threonine-923 in the tethered agonist of Lphn3 to glycine inhibited autoproteolysis while maintaining proper folding of the receptor.
source: Previous studies showed that replacing threonine-838 in the tethered agonist of Lphn1 or threonine-923 in the tethered agonist of Lphn3 to glycine inhibited autoproteolysis while maintaining proper folding of the receptor (Araç et al., 2012; Kordon et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Araç et al., 2012; Kordon et al., 2023

claim: Lphn2_T829G was cleavage resistant.
source: Thus, we mutated the analogous threonine-829 in Lphn2 (Lphn2_T829G) and confirmed that Lphn2_T829G was cleavage resistant using immunoblotting (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Lphn2_T829G is expressed on the cell surface at a comparable level as Lphn2 wild-type.
source: We also validated that Lphn2_T829G is expressed on the cell surface at a comparable level as Lphn2 wild-type (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Full-length Lphn2_T829G had significantly impaired SRE response compared to wild-type Lphn2.
source: Full-length Lphn2_T829G had significantly impaired SRE response compared to wild-type Lphn2, consistent with diminished exposure of the tethered agonist in the absence of cleavage; however, when we tested Lphn2-CTF_T829G, which lacked the entire NTF up to the GPS cleavage site, we observed SRE levels comparable to Lphn2-CTF suggesting that the mutated tethered agonist is fully active if exposed.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Lphn2-CTF_T829G, which lacked the entire NTF up to the GPS cleavage site, had SRE levels comparable to Lphn2-CTF.
source: Full-length Lphn2_T829G had significantly impaired SRE response compared to wild-type Lphn2, consistent with diminished exposure of the tethered agonist in the absence of cleavage; however, when we tested Lphn2-CTF_T829G, which lacked the entire NTF up to the GPS cleavage site, we observed SRE levels comparable to Lphn2-CTF suggesting that the mutated tethered agonist is fully active if exposed.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: The T829G-CTF retained BRET signaling comparable to wild-type Lphn2-CTF for Gα12 and Gα13.
source: The T829G-CTF retained BRET signaling comparable to wild-type Lphn2-CTF for Gα12 and Gα13, with no discernable BRET response for Gαs, Gαi1, or Gαq (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Lphn2_T829G is resistant to autoproteolytic cleavage but maintains a functional tethered agonist.
source: Taken together, these data supported that Lphn2_T829G is resistant to autoproteolytic cleavage but maintains a functional tethered agonist.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: Lphn2_T829G-expressing proximal CA1 axons did not show highly enriched targeting to a specific region of the subiculum.
source: Overall, Lphn2_T829G-expressing proximal CA1 axons did not show highly enriched targeting to a specific region of the subiculum, as observed for control proximal CA1 axons or Lphn2 misexpressing proximal CA1 axons, which preferentially target distal and proximal subiculum, respectively (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E

claim: Compared to the control there was a significant increase in the fraction of axon intensity in the proximal subiculum in Cre-Lphn2_T829G animals.
source: However, compared to the control there was a significant increase in the fraction of axon intensity in the proximal subiculum in Cre-Lphn2_T829G animals, even though this mistargeting was not as pronounced as seen with wild-type Cre-Lphn2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2.).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: Autoproteolysis is not absolutely required for Lphn2 misexpression-induced miswiring of proximal CA1 axons.
source: The intermediate gain-of-function phenotypes of misexpressing Lphn2_T829G compared to misexpressing wild-type Lphn2 or tethered agonist-deficient (and non-cleavable) Lphn2 suggest that autoproteolysis is not absolutely required for Lphn2 misexpression-induced miswiring of proximal CA1 axons.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4

claim: Misexpression of Lphn2 in distal subiculum target neurons causes proximal CA1 axons to avoid this area.
source: We previously showed that misexpression of Lphn2 in distal subiculum target neurons causes proximal CA1 axons to avoid this area, suggesting that Lphn2 acts cell non-autonomously as a repulsive ligand in directing target selection of proximal CA1 axons (Pederick et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pederick et al., 2021

claim: When either GFP-Lphn2_F831A/M835A or GFP-Lphn2_T829G were expressed in the distal subiculum, there was a significant decrease in axon intensity in GFP positive regions compared to GFP.
source: When either GFP-Lphn2_F831A/M835A or GFP-Lphn2_T829G were expressed in the distal subiculum, we also observed a significant decrease in axon intensity in GFP positive regions compared to GFP (Figure 5D, E and F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D).

claim: The decrease in axon intensity in GFP positive regions for GFP-Lphn2_F831A/M835A or GFP-Lphn2_T829G was not significantly different from GFP-Lphn2 animals.

claim: Neither tethered agonist activity nor autoproteolysis is required for Lphn2's cell-non-autonomous role as a ligand in the neural circuit assembly.
source: These findings suggest that neither tethered agonist activity nor autoproteolysis is required for Lphn2's cell-non-autonomous role as a ligand in the neural circuit assembly.

claim: Lphn2 G protein signaling is required in axons but not target neurons during precise circuit assembly.

claim: Gα13 binds to and activates p115RhoGEF, an exchange factor for and activator of the small GTPase RhoA.
source: Gα12/Gα13 are known to regulate Rho GTPase; for example, Gα13 binds to and activates p115RhoGEF, an exchange factor for and activator of the small GTPase RhoA (Kozasa et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kozasa et al., 2011

claim: RhoA activation is known to cause growth cone collapse and neuronal process retraction via its regulation of the actin-myosin contractility.
source: RhoA activation is known to cause growth cone collapse and neuronal process retraction via its regulation of the actin-myosin contractility (Luo, 2002; Spillane and Gallo, 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Luo, 2002; Spillane and Gallo, 2014

claim: Teneurins are known to undergo proteolytic cleavage at its extracellular domain.
source: Other potential mechanisms to disassemble the extracellular binding complex include Ten3 cleavage (teneurins are known to also undergo proteolytic cleavage at its extracellular domain; Sita et al., 2019), endocytosis of the adhesion complex as in the case of ephrin/Eph receptor (Egea and Klein, 2007), or forces produced by actin-myosin contractility in axon terminals induced by repulsive signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sita et al., 2019

claim: Crystal structures of GAIN domains from Lphn1 and ADGRB3 (BAI3) revealed that in an intact aGPCR, the tethered agonist is buried as a β-strand in the GAIN domain, forming an extensive network of conserved hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic side chains.
source: Crystal structures of GAIN domains from Lphn1 and ADGRB3 (BAI3) (Araç et al., 2012), ADGRG1 (GPR56) (Salzman et al., 2016), and ADGRG6 (GPR126) (Leon et al., 2020), revealed that in an intact aGPCR, the tethered agonist is buried as a β-strand in the GAIN domain, forming an extensive network of conserved hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic side chains.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Araç et al., 2012; Salzman et al., 2016; Leon et al., 2020

claim: Several studies have reported that naturally cleavage-resistant aGPCRs can still function.
source: However, several studies have reported that naturally cleavage-resistant aGPCRs can still function (Liebscher et al., 2014; Wilde et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liebscher et al., 2014; Wilde et al., 2016

claim: The structure of autoproteolysis-deficient ADGRF1 supported the possibility of the cleavage-independent manner of receptor activation.
source: While most discussions from the structural aGPCR studies argued that NTF dissociation is required for tethered agonist interaction with the receptor, the structure of autoproteolysis-deficient ADGRF1 supported the possibility of the cleavage-independent manner of receptor activation (Qu et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Qu et al., 2022

claim: The density for the tethered agonist of ADGRF1 was well-resolved and bound in an α-helical structure within the orthosteric site of the 7TM bundle.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Qu et al., 2022 in the preceding sentence

claim: ADGRF1 was observed to be bound to a miniGi1, supporting that receptor cleavage and tethered agonist exposure are not absolutely required for G protein coupling.
source: This interaction was like that of the cleaved structures, and ADGRF1 was also observed to be bound to a miniGi1, supporting that receptor cleavage and tethered agonist exposure are not absolutely required for G protein coupling.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Qu et al., 2022 in the preceding context

claim: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of spontaneous tethered agonist exposure were recently reported for five intact aGPCR homologs (ADGRB3, ADGRE2, ADGRE5, ADGRG1, and Lphn1).
source: In fact, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of spontaneous tethered agonist exposure were recently reported for five intact aGPCR homologs (ADGRB3, ADGRE2, ADGRE5, ADGRG1, and Lphn1) (Beliu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Beliu et al., 2021

claim: Tethered agonist exposure occurs due to the high intrinsic flexibility of the GAIN domain.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Beliu et al., 2021 in the preceding sentence

claim: Large portions (+6 residues) of the tethered agonist can become solvent accessible in the context of the GAIN domain.

source: Lphn2 was amplified from cDNA isolated from the P8 mouse hippocampus.

claim: Full-length Lphn2 and Lphn2-CTF ran at the expected truncated position (~72 kDa) suggesting that full-length Lphn2 undergoes normal proteolytic cleavage.
source: We tested the expression of these constructs in mammalian cells using immunoblotting and showed that both full-length Lphn2 and Lphn2-CTF ran at the expected truncated position (~72 kDa) suggesting that full-length Lphn2 undergoes normal proteolytic cleavage (Figure 2B).

claim: Ectopically expressing wild-type Lphn2 in proximal CA1 axons causes their mistargeting to the proximal subiculum.
source: By contrast, when Lphn2 was misexpressed in proximal CA1 (Cre-Lphn2), Cre+ proximal CA1 axons targeted the most proximal parts of the subiculum (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Proximal CA1 axons misexpressing Lphn2 are located significantly more in the proximal third of the subiculum and significantly less in the distal third of the subiculum when compared to control axons.
source: Proximal CA1 axons misexpressing Lphn2 are located significantly more in the proximal third of the subiculum and significantly less in the distal third of the subiculum when compared to control axons (Figure 1H).

claim: The phenotype observed when overexpressing Lphn2 in pCA1 axons is more severe than that observed when Ten3 is deleted.
source: Importantly, the phenotype observed when overexpressing Lphn2 in pCA1 axons is more severe than that observed when Ten3 is deleted (Berns et al., 2018), suggesting that mistargeting is not caused by disruption of Ten3 expression alone.
